summary: The note retells the folklore of the Weeping Stone in the remote village of Eldergrove, as told to the narrator by matriarch Eileen Bramblewood on September 3, 2023. The stone carries the curse of Isobel's grief after her love Collin Redwood was conscripted into war and she died of fever and despair. Anyone approaching it with a heavy heart has their sorrows magnified and is unable to leave. The legend endures through oral retelling and art, serving as a symbol of love, loss and village identity.
one_line: Legend of Eldergrove's Weeping Stone, cursed with maiden Isobel's grief, which traps sorrowful visitors and endures as village heritage.
key_facts: Eileen Bramblewood, matriarch of Eldergrove, first recounted the legend of the Weeping Stone to the narrator on September 3, 2023.
The legend centers on a young maiden, Isobel, whose love, Collin Redwood, was forcibly conscripted into a war.
Collin left on the 15th of September, the day Isobel's heart was said to have shattered.
Isobel wept by a solitary stone on the riverbank beneath ancient oaks until she had no tears left.
The spirits of Eldergrove forest, moved by her lament, made the stone an eternal receptacle of her sorrow, creating the Weeping Stone.
Collin returned in a grey October to learn Isobel had died of fever and despair in his absence.
The curse ensnares anyone who approaches with a heavy heart, magnifying their sorrows so they cannot leave; Collin Redwood was its first victim.
Children dare each other to approach the stone but retreat as the air turns melancholic.
Nigel Farthington, eldest son of Eldergrove's carpenter, said his grandfather ventured too close in the winter of 2045 and felt inexplicable sadness while the river iced over.
Local artist Ava Green unveiled a bronze sculpture honoring the Weeping Stone on the eve of September 30, 2063.
Ava Green described her work as a silent dialogue between past and present.
The Eldergrove community is wary of the stone's past but acknowledges its role in their collective history, with figures like Eileen Bramblewood safeguarding the story orally.
